WEST CAPE FARMERS' WATER WARS

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
West Coast farmers not only have to contend with Eskom and fuel price increases, but drought has seen them cut back production for the last 2 years...now their neighbours divert their water

Unique Selling Point:
As the Western Cape drought continues, it's high drama for farmers on the West Coast, where jobs and lives are at stake. What will the impact on the economy really be if the rains don't come, and other plans for salvation don't succeed? Farmers are under serious pressure from increases in things like electricity and the fuel price, let alone the lack of water. We examine the big picture by looking at one municipality and its tireless battles as a case study.
The Matzikama Local Municipality is waging the battle for water on a variety of fronts. It has an ambitious plan to extract water from an aquifer, but money is scarce. It is also tackling farmers upstream on the Olifants River for allegedly illegally damming up the river and taking more than their fair share.

Summary:
In the Matzikama municipality in the Western Cape, farmers have to plant their crops by October, but they are horribly short on water. The drought is hitting everyone hard, but for these farmers and their workers, their livelihood is disappearing. Depression has landed some in psychiatric institutions, and there have been suicides.
Thousands of jobs stand to be lost if the farmers can only produce a fraction of their usual crops - the prediction right now if things don't change. Companies such as Tiger Brands, which has a tomato processing plant in the area, have warned of major job losses.
Meanwhile, farmers are fighting about the little bit of water that's left. Those in Matzikama and the Clanwilliam area are accusing farmers upstream in the Citrusdal area of illegally damming up the Olifants River and robbing them of their fair share of the water. They have asked the Department of Water and Sanitation to take action, but to no avail yet. The Citrusdal Water Users Association has allegedly walked out of meetings meant to find a solution, and stated that the downstream farmers are not their concern.
The Matzikama municipality has declared a disaster area, in the hopes of getting funding from donors and national government. They have a plan, but no way yet of pulling it off.
Matzikama wants to access an underground aquifer, something they need R100 million for. They are currently raising funds for this.
Meanwhile, farmers are also being squeezed from other sides with electricity price increases and fuel getting more expensive.

Press Release:


Farmers are facing a tough battle against the drought in the Western Cape. Factories are closed, trucks are parked and seasonal workers are sitting at home. If farmers don't get help soon, the recovery could take years. Carte Blanche asks: What will the impact on the economy really be if the rains don't come, and alternative plans don't succeed?

Script:


VO: The water crisis in Cape Town and other Western Cape towns is by now well-known. For farming communities across the Western Cape, things are just as desperate, if not more so.

WILFRED STEPHAN, VREDENDAL FARMER: The growth you’re seeing comes from the winter’s reserves but by February it will definitely be a totally different story.

VO: Wilfred Stephan is one of the largest table grape producers in Vredendal. The town lies in the Olifants River valley on the West Coast.

JOHN WEBB LINK: The catchment for the Olifants River is in the mountains behind me, known as the Cederberg. It's the lifeblood of an already arid area and every drop is carefully monitored.

VO: The Olifants River, stretching from the mountains behind Citrusdal northwards to the Atlantic Ocean, is a mere shadow of what it looks like when the rains are good. The winter rains have been disappointing for three years now. The vineyards and evergreen citrus still looks healthy now but without water, there is little hope.

MARIE ANDREAS, VREDENDAL FARM WORKER: If you look out and you look over the plains, you can see it’s not going that well. It’s not nice to see it like this.

VO: Already, there’s less work for locals like Marie Andreas, a single mom who’s raised three kids on a farm worker salary in Vredendal. Her employer has had to reduce working hours to two and a half days a week.

MARIE ANDREAS, VREDENDAL FARM WORKER: We work fewer hours now. With fewer hours, we also don’t earn much.
JOHN WEBB: So how much do you earn now?
MARIE ANDREAS, VREDENDAL FARM WORKER: R285.
JOHN WEBB: Per week?
MARIE ANDREAS, VREDENDAL FARM WORKER: Per week. It’s rather tough, because having a child at school, as a single woman, is not so easy.

VO: She still has a roof over her head for now. But it’s a different story for seasonal workers.

MARIE ANDREAS, VREDENDAL FARM WORKER: The boss has not really taken on many seasonal workers. He hardly has work for us.

VO: Near the end of last year, Vredendal saw its first protest for jobs.

JOHN WEBB LINK: People tend to see a drought as a natural phenomenon only, ignoring the broader economic and social impacts...but those are already keenly being felt in this part of the Western Cape...with business closing, jobs being lost, and already a spike in crime...

VO: The largest wine cellar in the southern hemisphere, located in the town, says that production could be down 50% or more by month end. In nearby Lutzville, a major tomato paste factory has closed down for the time being. This year’s rooibos harvest, a crop unique to the Western Cape and largely drought resistant, will likely be reduced.

JOHN WEBB: This is almost a microcosm on what is going to happen across the entire province.

WILFRED STEPHAN, VREDENDAL FARMER: I farm with table grapes. So if I don’t have table grapes, who will the carton factory make cartons for? If we don’t have wine grapes, for which factory will they produce bottles? So the cold room has to retrench its workers, the truck drivers will have no work and if you can’t load freight on a ship, what’s going to happen at the harbour with the harbour’s people? So, what’s happening in Matzikama will also spill over to the city.

VO: The Matzikama Local Municipality consists of 18 towns. 80% of the economy and around 14 000 jobs rely on farming, but farmers now get less than 20% of their usual water supply.

JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS ASSOCIATION: Ja, there are 860 farmers here. A lot of cash crops too.

VO: Johan Matthee heads the water users’ association, which polices government’s water quotas.

JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS ASSOCIATION: We’re concentrating on the permanent crops. We try and save some of that. But what do you with 17% of your water, you can only save so much permanent crops…

VO: The towns are watered by an ageing canal system fed from the Clanwilliam Dam, in the Olifants River. But it’s time for desperate measures.

JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS ASSOCIATION: We’re stopping the channel at the end of March and the main reason is… is, there’s no water to transport the water, there’s no water for that.

JOHN WEBB: So you need a flow of water to drive the water that you are providing through the channel.

JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS ASSOCIATION: That’s correct... at the end of March we stop and then every third week, we’re going to start up the channel in trying to give the towns some drinking water and some of the farms.

VO: Matzikama municipal manager Danie Lubbe.

DANIE LUBBE, MATZIKAMA MUNICIPAL MANAGER: As we stand today the Clanwilliam dam that is our main source of water and agriculture stands at a level of 36%. That compares to 96% exactly the same date a year ago. Our hottest months are lying ahead.

VO: That was last year. The dam level is now at 21%. There would have been more water stored up if the dam had been expanded as planned.

JOHN WEBB LINK: The drought is first and foremost a natural disaster, but the extent of the damage that it has caused and is yet to cause to the economy and to people’s lives is in no small measure man-made -- the Clanwilliam Dam is a perfect example.

VO: The Department of Water and Sanitation’s construction unit started the work, but it stopped when minister Nomvula Mokonyane decided the job must be put out to tender. DA shadow minister of Water and Sanitation Leon Basson investigated the delays.

LEON BASSON, DA SHADOW MINISTER FOR WATER AND SANITATION: They started in 2014 with the new project to...to add another 30 metres to the dam, which was approved in 2010. And in 2015 the Minister just stopped the project.

JOHN WEBB: Do you know why?

LEON BASSON, DA SHADOW MINISTER FOR WATER AND SANITATION: There is no funding to complete the dam… they stopped the construction unit that was on site after they have established the site… The Minister decided to go out on tender. The tender is closed in November 2016 and nobody is on site and we’ve still got 53 construction unit people staying around Clanwilliam costing the ratepayers R2½ million a month.

JOHN WEBB: R2½ million a month for workers that are essentially doing nothing.

LEON BASSON, DA SHADOW MINISTER FOR WATER AND SANITATION: Nothing. They come in at the morning. They sign up and they go home.

JOHN WEBB: What an extraordinary waste of money...

VO: Tax payers have already forked out R131.9 million for site establishment and R550 million to divert the road and expropriate the land.

LEON BASSON, DA SHADOW MINISTER FOR WATER AND SANITATION: Why is the Minister opting for contractors while she has got 3 200 workers within a construction unit that could do the work. Most of the construction unit’s equipment is on site.

VO: In March last year, the minister said her department was still evaluating the tenders. The Department of Water and Sanitation would not speak to us and did not respond to questions about the project.

VO: Before reaching the dam, the Olifants River flows through Citrusdal, where farmers have built private dams to store water. Citrusdal Water Users Association chairman and citrus farmer Boet Mouton says they’re installing hi-tech monitoring to manage quotas.

BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: We should try and manage the water...as fair as possible.

JOHN WEBB: There are some farmers downstream who point fingers at you guys and say you’re diverting water before it gets to us and as a result we have less in our dam.

BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: We don’t have an upstream dam...we do have off site private dams. The total storage for Citrusdal private dams that we have on record is about 10 to 11% of the total Clanwilliam dam storage. That is all storage these farmers have and that’s that they put up with private capital. We’ve had 45, 46% of our annual rainfall this year. Last year in the middle of the drought the Clanwilliam dam still got filled. This year unfortunately not. But there’s only so much that Citrusdal can abstract and that is that 10%. The rest goes through. So it’s rainfall issue.

VO: The Mouton family business was better prepared than most for the lean years.

BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: John, I must… I must thank the previous generation before me. They always told me Boet the next drought is going to come, be prepared. In the previous drought we drilled a number of boreholes and looked for groundwater which we never used. We just keep it in reserve for droughts.

VO: Years of good exchange rates and booming citrus exports left them with the cash to quickly put up hi-tech drip irrigation and nets to reduce their water use by 40%.

HENDRIK CLOETE: You have to water the root zone only and not allow water to be lost.

BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: Agriculture especially in the Western Cape have a duty to be a leader in terms of water consumption. We’re the biggest user of water...we have to use this drought to think long term and say what is the solution that we’re not in this situation again?

JOHN WEBB: ’n Boer maak ’n plan, as they say.

BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: We… we hope the rain come soon enough that we don’t run out of plans.

VO: Throughout the area, farmers are brainstorming solutions. Near the ocean in Lutzville, one farmer set up a reverse osmosis plant to make the salty water from his boreholes usable to save some of his crops. With funding from local and provincial government, the Matzikama municipality sunk boreholes to secure drinking water. Now they’re racing against time to raise up to R40 million needed for an ambitious plan to extract underground water to keep the agriculture going.

DANIE LUBBE, MATZIKAMA MUNICIPAL MANAGER: What we did is immediately declared a disaster situation for our municipality. We’ve also then immediately established a disaster fund for the municipality. That’s all dedicated to agriculture.

VO: Test boreholes have found water at a depth of 100 to 300 metres. The municipality has asked provincial and national government and even the private sector for help and some R5 million promised by the Western Cape government is expected by the end of the month. In the meantime, the municipality has started drilling in the hopes that the money will come -- it will take weeks for these boreholes to become operational.

JOHN WEBB: Danie, there’s no question that you are being as proactive as you can be, but is it enough?

DANIE LUBBE, MATZIKAMA MUNICIPAL MANAGER: We really need to be supported by national government and the national department of water affairs and sanitation. And that is really where the problems lie.


PROMOS

VO: The effects of the drought are most keenly felt in the Western Cape, but the broader economic and social impacts will eventually be felt across the entire country.

15 secs
JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION: What do you with 17% of your water, you can only save so much permanent crops.
VO: As the drought persists, farmers on the West Coast are not only losing crops -- the livelihood of everyone in the area is at stake.

15 secs
VO: The drought in the Western Cape is forcing farmers to ask for support, but in the meantime they are making innovative plans.
BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION: Agriculture especially in the Western Cape have a duty to be a leader in terms of water consumption. We have to use this drought to think long-term.

VO: Johan Matthee heads the water users’ association, which polices government’s water quotas. JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS ASSOCIATION: We’re concentrating on the permanent crops. We try and save some of that. But what do you with 17% of your water, you can only save so much permanent crops… VO: The towns are watered by an ageing canal system fed from the Clanwilliam Dam, in the Olifants River. But it’s time for desperate measures. JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS ASSOCIATION: We’re stopping the channel at the end of March and the main reason is… is, there’s no water to transport the water, there’s no water for that. JOHN WEBB: So you need a flow of water to drive the water that you are providing through the channel. JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS ASSOCIATION: That’s correct... at the end of March we stop and then every third week, we’re going to start up the channel in trying to give the towns some drinking water and some of the farms. VO: Matzikama municipal manager Danie Lubbe. DANIE LUBBE, MATZIKAMA MUNICIPAL MANAGER: As we stand today the Clanwilliam dam that is our main source of water and agriculture stands at a level of 36%. That compares to 96% exactly the same date a year ago. Our hottest months are lying ahead. VO: That was last year. The dam level is now at 21%. There would have been more water stored up if the dam had been expanded as planned. JOHN WEBB LINK: The drought is first and foremost a natural disaster, but the extent of the damage that it has caused and is yet to cause to the economy and to people’s lives is in no small measure man-made -- the Clanwilliam Dam is a perfect example. VO: The Department of Water and Sanitation’s construction unit started the work, but it stopped when minister Nomvula Mokonyane decided the job must be put out to tender. DA shadow minister of Water and Sanitation Leon Basson investigated the delays. LEON BASSON, DA SHADOW MINISTER FOR WATER AND SANITATION: They started in 2014 with the new project to...to add another 30 metres to the dam, which was approved in 2010. And in 2015 the Minister just stopped the project. JOHN WEBB: Do you know why? LEON BASSON, DA SHADOW MINISTER FOR WATER AND SANITATION: There is no funding to complete the dam… they stopped the construction unit that was on site after they have established the site… The Minister decided to go out on tender. The tender is closed in November 2016 and nobody is on site and we’ve still got 53 construction unit people staying around Clanwilliam costing the ratepayers R2½ million a month. JOHN WEBB: R2½ million a month for workers that are essentially doing nothing. LEON BASSON, DA SHADOW MINISTER FOR WATER AND SANITATION: Nothing. They come in at the morning. They sign up and they go home. JOHN WEBB: What an extraordinary waste of money... VO: Tax payers have already forked out R131.9 million for site establishment and R550 million to divert the road and expropriate the land. LEON BASSON, DA SHADOW MINISTER FOR WATER AND SANITATION: Why is the Minister opting for contractors while she has got 3 200 workers within a construction unit that could do the work. Most of the construction unit’s equipment is on site. VO: In March last year, the minister said her department was still evaluating the tenders. The Department of Water and Sanitation would not speak to us and did not respond to questions about the project. VO: Before reaching the dam, the Olifants River flows through Citrusdal, where farmers have built private dams to store water. Citrusdal Water Users Association chairman and citrus farmer Boet Mouton says they’re installing hi-tech monitoring to manage quotas. BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: We should try and manage the water...as fair as possible. JOHN WEBB: There are some farmers downstream who point fingers at you guys and say you’re diverting water before it gets to us and as a result we have less in our dam. BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: We don’t have an upstream dam...we do have off site private dams. The total storage for Citrusdal private dams that we have on record is about 10 to 11% of the total Clanwilliam dam storage. That is all storage these farmers have and that’s that they put up with private capital. We’ve had 45, 46% of our annual rainfall this year. Last year in the middle of the drought the Clanwilliam dam still got filled. This year unfortunately not. But there’s only so much that Citrusdal can abstract and that is that 10%. The rest goes through. So it’s rainfall issue. VO: The Mouton family business was better prepared than most for the lean years. BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: John, I must… I must thank the previous generation before me. They always told me Boet the next drought is going to come, be prepared. In the previous drought we drilled a number of boreholes and looked for groundwater which we never used. We just keep it in reserve for droughts. VO: Years of good exchange rates and booming citrus exports left them with the cash to quickly put up hi-tech drip irrigation and nets to reduce their water use by 40%. HENDRIK CLOETE: You have to water the root zone only and not allow water to be lost. BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: Agriculture especially in the Western Cape have a duty to be a leader in terms of water consumption. We’re the biggest user of water...we have to use this drought to think long term and say what is the solution that we’re not in this situation again? JOHN WEBB: ’n Boer maak ’n plan, as they say. BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION AND CITRUS FARMER: We… we hope the rain come soon enough that we don’t run out of plans. VO: Throughout the area, farmers are brainstorming solutions. Near the ocean in Lutzville, one farmer set up a reverse osmosis plant to make the salty water from his boreholes usable to save some of his crops. With funding from local and provincial government, the Matzikama municipality sunk boreholes to secure drinking water. Now they’re racing against time to raise up to R40 million needed for an ambitious plan to extract underground water to keep the agriculture going. DANIE LUBBE, MATZIKAMA MUNICIPAL MANAGER: What we did is immediately declared a disaster situation for our municipality. We’ve also then immediately established a disaster fund for the municipality. That’s all dedicated to agriculture. VO: Test boreholes have found water at a depth of 100 to 300 metres. The municipality has asked provincial and national government and even the private sector for help and some R5 million promised by the Western Cape government is expected by the end of the month. In the meantime, the municipality has started drilling in the hopes that the money will come -- it will take weeks for these boreholes to become operational. JOHN WEBB: Danie, there’s no question that you are being as proactive as you can be, but is it enough? DANIE LUBBE, MATZIKAMA MUNICIPAL MANAGER: We really need to be supported by national government and the national department of water affairs and sanitation. And that is really where the problems lie. PROMOS 10 secs VO: The effects of the drought are most keenly felt in the Western Cape, but the broader economic and social impacts will eventually be felt across the entire country. 15 secs JOHAN MATTHEE, LOWER OLIFANTS RIVER WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION: What do you with 17% of your water, you can only save so much permanent crops. VO: As the drought persists, farmers on the West Coast are not only losing crops -- the livelihood of everyone in the area is at stake. 15 secs VO: The drought in the Western Cape is forcing farmers to ask for support, but in the meantime they are making innovative plans. BOET MOUTON, CITRUSDAL WATER USERS' ASSOCIATION: Agriculture especially in the Western Cape have a duty to be a leader in terms of water consumption. We have to use this drought to think long-term.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): West Coast farmers not only have to contend with Eskom and fuel price increases, but drought has seen them cut back production for the last 2 years...now their neighbours divert their water
metadata.Unique Selling Point: As the Western Cape drought continues, it's high drama for farmers on the West Coast, where jobs and lives are at stake. What will the impact on the economy really be if the rains don't come, and other plans for salvation don't succeed? Farmers are under serious pressure from increases in things like electricity and the fuel price, let alone the lack of water. We examine the big picture by looking at one municipality and its tireless battles as a case study. The Matzikama Local Municipality is waging the battle for water on a variety of fronts. It has an ambitious plan to extract water from an aquifer, but money is scarce. It is also tackling farmers upstream on the Olifants River for allegedly illegally damming up the river and taking more than their fair share.
metadata.Summary: In the Matzikama municipality in the Western Cape, farmers have to plant their crops by October, but they are horribly short on water. The drought is hitting everyone hard, but for these farmers and their workers, their livelihood is disappearing. Depression has landed some in psychiatric institutions, and there have been suicides. Thousands of jobs stand to be lost if the farmers can only produce a fraction of their usual crops - the prediction right now if things don't change. Companies such as Tiger Brands, which has a tomato processing plant in the area, have warned of major job losses. Meanwhile, farmers are fighting about the little bit of water that's left. Those in Matzikama and the Clanwilliam area are accusing farmers upstream in the Citrusdal area of illegally damming up the Olifants River and robbing them of their fair share of the water. They have asked the Department of Water and Sanitation to take action, but to no avail yet. The Citrusdal Water Users Association has allegedly walked out of meetings meant to find a solution, and stated that the downstream farmers are not their concern. The Matzikama municipality has declared a disaster area, in the hopes of getting funding from donors and national government. They have a plan, but no way yet of pulling it off. Matzikama wants to access an underground aquifer, something they need R100 million for. They are currently raising funds for this. Meanwhile, farmers are also being squeezed from other sides with electricity price increases and fuel getting more expensive.
